body.text: A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) can earn Canada's enhanced 35% SR&ED investment tax credit, fully refundable on current expenditures, on up to $6,000,000 of qualified spending for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. This limit phases out as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada rises from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 under the Income Tax Act.

Canada’s flagship federal innovation incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—underwent its most significant statutory expansion in over a decade on March 26, 2026, when Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the enacted legislation doubles the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), expands the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extends access to the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) based on a three-year average annual gross revenue test, and restores the eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, effective April 1, 2026 (and formally announced on April 8, 2026), the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval process (Form T1322) that provides upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cuts post-filing expenditure review processing times in half from 180 days to 90 days. At the provincial level, Quebec enacted a sweeping structural reform for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing eight legacy R&D tax measures (including the former R&D salary and wages credit under section 1029.7) and replacing them with the unified, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold (at least $50,000) and 20% on excess spending.
1. Executive Summary and Program Scale

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program is the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and experimental development in Canada. Unlike discretionary government grants that are constrained by fixed parliamentary appropriations and competitive intake windows, the SR&ED program is an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) alongside tax policy oversight from the Department of Finance Canada. Any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs qualifying SR&ED work in Canada—and files the prescribed technical and financial forms within the strict 18-month statutory reporting deadline—is entitled to two distinct, interlocking tax incentives:

items: Immediate or Indefinite Income Tax Deduction (Subsection 37(1)): Claimants may pool allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures in a dedicated tax pool under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, allowing them to deduct up to 100% of those available expenditures against current-year business income or carry any undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years.

SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Subsections 127(5) and 127(9)): Claimants earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on their qualified SR&ED expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year, ranging from a basic rate of 15% (generally non-refundable for large corporations, non-CCPCs, non-ECPCs, and expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit, though 40% refundable for qualifying CCPCs, individuals, and certain trusts) to an enhanced rate of 35% (100% refundable on current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount [PPA], and 40% refundable on capital expenditures, for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations [ECPCs]). Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable.

body.text: Government figures compiled in industry analyses of CRA program data underscore the expanding macroeconomic footprint of the incentive. During fiscal year 2024–2025, the CRA delivered $4.5 billion in SR&ED ITCs to more than 19,000 claimants across over 22,000 processed claims. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, industry reporting of CRA data indicates $4.9 billion in investment tax credits claimed and $4.6 billion allowed—representing a cumulative climb of roughly 50% in annual credit value since fiscal year 2022. Furthermore, according to CRA reporting data summarized by industry analysts for the most recent reporting year, roughly 96% of processed SR&ED claims resulted in allowed tax credits: specifically, the CRA accepted 90% of SR&ED claims entirely as filed, accepted an additional 6% following technical or financial modifications, and denied only 4%.

body.text: 2. Legislative Architecture and Statutory Definitions
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal gateway to all federal—and virtually all provincial and territorial—R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Prior to the late 1990s, this definition resided in section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations; after Northwest Hydraulic Consultants was decided, it was moved into subsection 248(1) of the Act without material alteration to its substantive scope. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and is structured into four positive inclusion limbs—paragraphs (a), (b), (c), and (d)—followed by seven explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k).
Core Research Categories: Paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), and (c)

To establish an eligible SR&ED project, the taxpayer must first conduct core scientific research or experimental development falling within one of the first three paragraphs of subsection 248(1). Basic research under paragraph (a) is defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. It is usually carried out in a laboratory setting, sometimes involves third-party payments to universities, research institutes, and consortia, and yields results that are typically published in scientific journals. Applied research under paragraph (b) is defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; like basic research, its findings may be published in scientific journals, but the inquiry is directed toward a defined practical use. Experimental development under paragraph (c)—which accounts for the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada—is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Notably, the statute explicitly covers incremental improvements to existing materials, devices, products, or processes, provided the work is experimental in nature and undertaken to achieve a technological advancement rather than routine development.
Eligible Support Work: Paragraph 248(1)(d)

Paragraph 248(1)(d) extends the definition of SR&ED to include work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Crucially, work falling within these eight categories is not SR&ED on its own. Under paragraph 248(1)(d), such work qualifies as SR&ED only where it is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. For example, computer programming, engineering design, or physical testing is ineligible if performed as a standalone commercial activity; however, when performed specifically to construct an experimental apparatus, test a hypothesis, or collect experimental data necessary to resolve a technological uncertainty in an active Canadian experimental development project, the activity qualifies as support work under paragraph 248(1)(d).
Explicitly Excluded Work: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)
Even where a taxpayer is conducting a valid SR&ED project, subsection 248(1) expressly excludes seven categories of commercial, routine, and non-scientific activities from the definition of SR&ED:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes (such as iterating a product's aesthetic form, surface finish, or visual proportions without resolving a technological uncertainty); and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives emphasize, the boundary between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "data collection" or "testing") and excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") turns entirely on purpose. Exclusions are considered only after it has been determined that eligible SR&ED work is taking place. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of supporting basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as support work under paragraph (d); if it is performed for routine quality assurance or normal business operations, it is excluded under paragraphs (f) and (k).
2.2 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From IC 86-4R3 and the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Framework

A thorough audit of Canadian SR&ED administration requires understanding how the CRA's administrative guidance has evolved alongside Tax Court jurisprudence. Prior to May 1985, guidance on whether work qualified as "applied or basic research" or "development" under the former Income Tax Regulations was provided in Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which the Department of Finance recognized was insufficient to explain eligible research and development. In the May 1985 Budget Papers, the Department of Finance announced amendments introducing the term "experimental development" to clarify the concept of development and explicitly exclude projects involving only routine engineering or routine development. Following a March 4, 1986 clarification from the Department of Finance, Revenue Canada and industry leaders co-developed Information Circular 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development), revised through IC 86-4R3 in 1994, which established three essential criteria for industrial SR&ED: (1) scientific or technological advancement, (2) scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) scientific and technical content (systematic investigation). Additionally, a 1992 clarification confirmed that experimental development work undertaken to achieve technological advancement to create or improve existing materials qualifies, whereas routine development work does not.

In May 1998, Judge Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada issued the landmark ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839), drawing from IC 86-4R3 to define the relationship between the statutory definition of SR&ED and five sequential criteria. The CRA formalized Judge Bowman's five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012, revised in 2015, and archived in 2021):

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In August 2021 (updated in July 2022), following a 2020 program modernization initiative, the CRA replaced the 2015 policy with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) and the five Northwest Hydraulic judicial criteria remain unchanged and binding in court, the current CRA guidelines organize the evaluation into two core requirements that encompass all five questions:

items: The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement): The work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. Technological uncertainty arises when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved due to an insufficiency in available scientific or technological knowledge (comprising both internal business knowledge and publicly accessible resources). Indicators of insufficient technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications do not conform to existing standards, too many variables or unknowns exist, parameters lie outside normal operating ranges, the problem is evolving, data is unavailable, interlocking constraints exist, or strict cost targets impose technological uncertainty. Conversely, if an uncertainty is circumvented via a workaround using available knowledge or standard routines, or if knowledge is merely acquired through training, hiring consultants, or purchasing proprietary know-how, the "Why" requirement is not met.

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search): The work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals (personnel with relevant qualifications and/or experience in science, technology, or engineering). This requires (i) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point for investigation, (ii) testing that hypothesis through experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as a result of testing), (iii) developing logical conclusions based on experimental or analytical results, and (iv) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

body.text: 2.3 Section 37: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act establishes the "pool" mechanism for deducting SR&ED expenditures when computing income from a business carried on in Canada. Rather than forcing taxpayers to amortize R&D outlays or deduct them strictly in the year incurred, subsection 37(1) aggregates eligible SR&ED expenditures into a cumulative pool calculated in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661. Where a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (such as a parent company), the SR&ED is considered related to the business of the claimant under subsection 37(1). By contrast, under subsection 37(2), current expenditures for SR&ED performed outside Canada cannot enter the subsection 37(1) pool, cannot be claimed on Form T661, and do not earn an ITC (except for permissible foreign salaries up to the 10% limit under subsection 37(1.5)), though they may be deducted directly when calculating current-year net income or loss.
Additions to the Section 37(1) Pool
Under subsection 37(1), the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is increased each taxation year by six statutory categories:

items: Paragraph 37(1)(a) — Current Expenditures: Allowable expenditures of a current nature incurred in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, comprising: the portion of salaries or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), including permissible foreign SR&ED salaries under subsection 37(1.5); the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED; equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, that qualify under the Traditional or Proxy Method (as well as pre-2014 lease costs); 100% of contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)); 100% of eligible third-party payments to corporations (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)) and approved entities (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)); and overhead expenditures when the Traditional Method is elected. Where the Proxy Method is elected, the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is not added to the subsection 37(1) pool; instead, actual overhead expenses are deducted as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1).

Paragraph 37(1)(b) — Capital Expenditures: Expenditures of a capital nature made after December 15, 2024 (as well as legacy capital acquired prior to 2014) to acquire new or used depreciable property (other than a building or leasehold interest in a building) intended to be used all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or to have 90% or more of its value consumed in SR&ED in Canada.

Paragraph 37(1)(c) — Repayments of Assistance: Repayments of government assistance or non-government assistance made in the year, to the extent that the assistance previously reduced the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

Paragraph 37(1)(c.1) — Negative Pool Balance Add-Back: Amounts included in the taxpayer's income in the preceding taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) due to a negative pool balance, resetting the opening pool balance to nil.
Amalgamation or Wind-Up Transfers: The pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures transferred from a predecessor or subsidiary corporation upon an amalgamation or wind-up.
Prior-Year ITC Recapture: The amount of SR&ED ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year (or added due to a partnership ITC recapture excess).

body.text: Reductions to the Section 37(1) Pool and Income Inclusion Mechanics
Under subsection 37(1), the deductible pool is decreased by:

items: Paragraph 37(1)(d) — Government and Non-Government Assistance: All government assistance (including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, super-allowance benefit amounts, grants, subsidies, and forgivable loans) and non-government assistance that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date in respect of SR&ED expenditures in the pool. Reductions apply on a project-by-project basis and can reduce a project's expenditures only to nil (any excess assistance is included in income). Proxy Method Exception: Because the PPA is not included in the subsection 37(1) pool, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the PPA does not reduce the deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(d); instead, that portion must be included in income in the year received under paragraph 12(1)(x).

Prior-Year Federal SR&ED ITC Used (Paragraph 12(1)(t) / Pool Reduction): Any SR&ED ITC used in the preceding taxation year (whether refunded in cash, applied against Part I tax payable, or carried back) reduces the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool in the following year (or is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(t)). If reductions cause the subsection 37(1) pool balance to become negative at the end of a taxation year, the negative balance must be brought into net income for tax purposes in that year under paragraph 12(1)(v), and is then added back under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) in the following year so that the opening pool balance is never negative.

Prior-Year Pool Deductions and Insolvency Deductions: Amounts deducted from the pool in previous years, as well as insolvency deductions claimed under section 61.3 in preceding years (up to the balance of the pool in that year).

body.text: Carryforward Rules, Partnerships, Rights Acquisition, and Loss Restriction Events

A positive balance in the subsection 37(1) pool of a corporation or individual does not expire and can be carried forward indefinitely to be deducted against business income in future taxation years. Utilizing an accumulated pool balance in a future year is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the expenditures comprising the pool were identified on time on Form T661 in the year incurred. However, a partnership is prohibited from carrying forward any balance in its subsection 37(1) pool; the pool balance must be deducted in full at the partnership level in calculating the partnership's net income for tax purposes in the year incurred. Furthermore, under subsection 37(4), no deduction is allowed for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED. Finally, if a corporate claimant or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), its subsection 37(1) pool is reduced and restricted under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h): pre-acquisition pool balances can only be reinstated and deducted in subsequent taxation years when the business to which the expenditure related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of income from that same business or a similar business.
3. Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Bill C-15 Reforms
3.1 The 2025–2026 Legislative Overhaul (Bill C-15)

Following proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (which initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit to $4,500,000) and enhanced in the 2025 Federal Budget, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. These statutory amendments are law and apply retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (and to depreciable capital property and leased equipment acquired after December 15, 2024).
3.2 Two-Tiered Federal ITC Rate Structure: 35% Enhanced vs. 15% Basic
Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, Canada operates a two-tiered federal SR&ED ITC rate structure:

items: The Enhanced 35% ITC Rate: Consisting of the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement, the 35% rate applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual Expenditure Limit—which is $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (up from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Eligible claimants for the 35% enhanced rate are qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).

The Basic 15% ITC Rate: Applies to (i) qualified SR&ED expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC that exceed its annual expenditure limit for the taxation year, (ii) all qualified SR&ED expenditures of other corporations (such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries and non-qualifying public corporations), and (iii) sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of partnerships, and beneficiaries of trusts (on their reasonably designated portion of trust SR&ED ITCs). Note that under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, no ITC may be earned in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from Part I tax (such as non-prescribed Crown corporations).

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's maximum $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. B. Gross Revenue Phase-Out Structure for ECPCs (and Electing CCPCs)

Unlike CCPCs (which default to prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) determine the gradual reduction of their $6,000,000 expenditure limit based on the average annual revenue of their preceding 3 fiscal years as reflected in their financial statements. If an ECPC is part of a consolidated group that prepares consolidated financial statements, the expenditure limit is shared among the members of the consolidated group and is calculated using the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the group for the preceding 3 fiscal years. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs may elect (using the prescribed form) to calculate their expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average annual gross revenue method—which requires totalling average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation in the associated group over the preceding 3 fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire period.

body.text: 4. Granular Audit of Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs)

To calculate a claim on Form T661, a taxpayer must first determine its allowable SR&ED expenditures (Part 3 of Form T661) and then adjust those figures to compute its Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Part 4 of Form T661) under subsection 127(9). Unlike the subsection 37(1) pool, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is calculated at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over to another taxation year.
4.1 Salaries and Wages (Directly Engaged, Support, Specified Employees, and Foreign Work)

Under subsection 248(1) and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Income Tax Act, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act, including fees for services not rendered in the course of business, but excluding superannuation/pension benefits or retiring allowances.
Inclusions and Exclusions in SR&ED Salaries and Wages

Eligible remuneration includes base salary or wages incurred on or in respect of SR&ED, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducements and non-competition payments, and (for employees other than specified employees) bonuses and remuneration based on profits. Cash outlays for employee benefits taxable under section 6 of the Act also qualify, and non-cash taxable benefits may be included if the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit can be claimed), and the actual costs are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense. Conversely, the employer's share of related employee benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and unpaid salary or wages (remuneration not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred) are strictly excluded from SR&ED salaries and wages.
"Directly Engaged" vs. Support, Supervisory, and Clerical Personnel

Whether an employee is "directly engaged in SR&ED" is determined by the actual tasks performed, not by the employee's job title. Directly engaged work encompasses hands-on work described in paragraphs (a) to (d) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1): preparing equipment and materials for tests and experiments, carrying out experiments and tests, collecting data, directing ongoing SR&ED activities, recording measurements and calculations, preparing computer programs, conducting engineering or design or mathematical analysis work, and performing support work that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

Managers and supervisors are considered directly engaged to the extent they are directly supervising ongoing SR&ED, directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED work (such as technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year, including assignment of technological personnel, job priorities, development of technological strategies, and quality of materials used), or providing direct technical input. Time spent on non-technological management activities or decision-making functions that do not directly influence the course of SR&ED—and work performed beyond first-line supervision without proof of duties directly engaged in SR&ED—does not qualify. Clerical and administrative staff are not considered directly engaged in SR&ED under the Proxy Method; under the Traditional Method, their salaries may qualify as overhead/other expenditures on Line 360 only if their non-technological duties aiding ongoing SR&ED satisfy both the "directly related" and "incremental" tests.
Specified Employee Restrictions (10% Shareholders and Non-Arm's-Length Employees)

A specified employee is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of a related corporation. Specified employees are subject to two strict statutory caps based on the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for Canada Pension Plan (CPP) purposes for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends:

items: Direct SR&ED Salary Pool Cap (5 × YMPE and No Bonuses): For a specified employee, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are completely excluded from SR&ED salary or wages. Furthermore, the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the YMPE (5 × YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Lesser of 75% of Base Salary or 2.5 × YMPE): Under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, the amount of salary or wages that a claimant can include in the salary base for a specified employee to calculate the 55% PPA is restricted to the lesser of (i) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior years' unpaid amounts paid in the year), or (ii) 2.5 times the YMPE prorated for the number of days of employment in the year (with no proration for the portion of the year the employee was not a specified employee):

body.text: Foreign SR&ED Work Limit (Subsection 37(1.5): The 10% Rule)

Under subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, claimants can include permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada—deeming them to be expenditures made in Canada that qualify for both the subsection 37(1) pool and the SR&ED ITC (including the PPA salary base)—up to a maximum of 10% of the total salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant, provided all four conditions are satisfied:

items: The SR&ED work outside Canada is directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (never by a contractor);
The employee performing the work is a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred;
The work is related to a business of the claimant; and
The foreign work forms part of the overall SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant.

body.text: Note that while the employee's permissible foreign salary qualifies up to the 10% limit, any associated foreign travel, hotel, and meal expenses for SR&ED work performed outside Canada are not deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1).
4.2 Overhead and Other Expenditures: The Proxy Method (55% PPA) vs. the Traditional Method
Claimants must elect on Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661 whether to compute SR&ED overhead using the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method for the taxation year.
A. The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(4))
Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% of the salary base since 2014.

Calculated in Part 5 of Form T661, the salary base consists of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (and permissible foreign SR&ED salaries), excluding for all employees: (i) taxable benefits under section 6, (ii) unpaid amounts from a prior year paid in the current taxation year (Line 310 of Form T661), (iii) remuneration based on profits, (iv) bonuses, and (v) employer-paid benefit contributions. The resulting PPA (55% of the salary base) is a notional amount included in qualified SR&ED expenditures solely to earn the SR&ED ITC. It is not included in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and is not deducted as an SR&ED expenditure; instead, the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA (such as office supplies, utilities, clerical support, and general-purpose office equipment or furniture) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) (with the exception of retiring allowances, which are deductible under the Traditional Method but not under the Proxy Method).

Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is subject to an Overall Cap designed to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted in the year:
Overall cap = A − B − C

Where A equals total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B equals deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED pool deduction per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts); and C equals expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as building rent). Usually, the Overall Cap will not restrict the 55% PPA if the claimant has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses (excluding the statutory deductions in B and C) for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
B. The Traditional Method (Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3))

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, no PPA or salary base is calculated. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate each overhead and other expenditure claimed on Line 360 of Form T661. Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, an expenditure of a current nature (or allocated portion thereof) qualifies as directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED) only if it satisfies both tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (excluding any indirect portions), requiring a direct linkage with no intervening step or intermediary between the expenditure and (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED; and
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

body.text: Qualifying Traditional Method overhead enters both the subsection 37(1) pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITCs. Examples include incremental utilities, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises/facilities/equipment, directly related and incremental clerical/administrative wages, moving expenses for relocating SR&ED employees within Canada (though travel costs for the hiring selection process do not qualify), and travel and lodging expenses in Canada to conduct testing at a customer location (or foreign travel to visit foreign customers with respect to SR&ED carried on in Canada where no foreign SR&ED work is performed). However, prescribed expenditures under the Regulations—including SR&ED claim preparation fees, general legal and accounting fees, interest and financing costs, entertainment, advertising/selling, membership dues, fines/penalties, and conference/convention costs—are excluded from earning ITCs even under the Traditional Method.
4.3 Subcontractors (Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length) and Third-Party Payments
Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (80% Inclusion Rule)
When a claimant (payer) contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf (where the payer controls the work and maintains exclusive rights to the results):

items: 100% of the current contract expenditure is included in the payer's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01); and
80% of the eligible contract expenditure is allowable as a qualified SR&ED expenditure for calculating the payer's ITC under subsection 127(9).

body.text: Where a contract with an arm's-length performer is for SR&ED only, the CRA does not look through the contract (except that prior to December 16, 2024, capital expenditures of the performer were looked through and excluded under subsection 37(14); for contract expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, payments are generally no longer reduced by non-current expenditures of the performer). If a claimant contracts out only support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)) to an arm's-length party, the payer can claim the contract amount only if the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED performed in Canada by or on behalf of the claimant; the arm's-length performer cannot claim SR&ED credits on standalone support work. Conversely, where an arm's-length performer carries out SR&ED on behalf of a Canadian payer, any contract payment received or receivable reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) (though it does not reduce the performer's subsection 37(1) deductible pool).
Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts and Form T1146 Transfers

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a person or partnership with whom it does not deal at arm's length (under section 251 of the ITA), the expenditures are allowable in the payer's subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but they are not qualified SR&ED expenditures for the payer's ITC calculation. Because payments received by a NAL performer are not defined as "contract payments," they do not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures. Consequently, the NAL performer can either claim the ITC itself or transfer all or a portion of its qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year (up to the contract amount) to the NAL payer under subsection 127(13) by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to transfer qualified expenditures incurred in respect of SR&ED contracts between persons not dealing at arm's length, reported on Line 540 of Form T661 by the performer). Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), a claimant cannot circumvent the NAL rules by inserting an arm's-length third party between a payer and a NAL performer if the main purpose of the arrangement is to obtain a qualified expenditure.
Third-Party Payments (Entities A to F)

Claimants may also make third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and 37(1)(a)(ii) to fund SR&ED in Canada where the SR&ED work is controlled by the performing organization rather than the payer. Only 80% of an eligible third-party payment is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes. Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, recipients are categorized as follows:

items: Entity A: A corporation resident in Canada;
Entity B: An approved association;
Entity C: An approved university, college, research institute, or similar institution;
Entity D: A non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada and exempt from tax;
Entity E: An approved organization (such as a granting council like NSERC) that makes payments to an association, institution, or corporation; and
Entity F: A corporation resident in Canada that is exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) of the Act (for payments from a corporate claimant).

body.text: To qualify, the claimant must retain documentation proving (i) to whom and for what the payments were made and the amount, (ii) that the payments were to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada, (iii) that the SR&ED relates to a business of the claimant, and (iv) that the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED (meaning the claimant gained the right to use the results in its business as a direct result of the payment). Payments in kind to a university or college are valued at fair market value (provided without conditions involving direct or indirect payments back to the claimant), whereas third-party payments used to acquire a building, a leasehold interest in a building, or building rental expense are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d).
4.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and Custom Products / Pilot Plants

Under both the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and paragraph 2900(2)(a)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)), current expenditures for the cost of materials may be claimed at 100% only in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—not when purchased or removed from inventory. When purchasing materials from a non-arm's-length supplier, the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes is restricted under subsection 127(11.6) to the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier, excluding any intercompany profit margin.

items: Materials Consumed: Materials are considered consumed if they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of the prosecution of SR&ED (such as components destroyed during testing, input materials rendered valueless in experimental production, or additional input materials beyond normal commercial requirements consumed due to SR&ED conducted during commercial production runs). If experimental production is sold for more than 10% of the original cost, the materials are considered not to have been consumed in SR&ED. Similarly, items that are consumed without ever being incorporated into a thing during the SR&ED process (general supplies) do not meet the definition of "materials for SR&ED".

Materials Transformed, Pilot Plants, and Custom Products: When materials for SR&ED are not rendered virtually valueless after the SR&ED, they may qualify as materials transformed in the year of transformation. Examples include materials incorporated into a pilot plant, custom product, or commercial asset where the material was transformed in or as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED, as well as input materials converted during experimental development with experimental production (ED+EP). Under the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, eligible expenditures when developing a pilot plant or custom commercial asset include the labour and materials consumed or transformed in resolving the technological uncertainties (calculated for a custom product or commercial asset as the total actual development costs minus the estimated costs normally associated with constructing the asset if the technology had already existed, plus the estimated cost of materials transformed in SR&ED). However, materials transformed into a property that is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use for 10% or more of its original cost within 20 taxation years are subject to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36).

body.text: 4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), Parliament restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Claimants and auditors must carefully distinguish these three regimes across the updated CRA policies published in May and June 2026:
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Line 390 of Form T661)

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (Traditional Method) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (Proxy Method), expenditures of a capital nature made after December 15, 2024, that result in the acquisition of depreciable property (within the meaning of subsection 13(21), available for use under subsection 37(1.2) after December 15, 2024) qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures on Line 390 of Form T661 if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either:

items: That the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada; or

That ASA (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (for example, property used in developing an asset that has less than 10% life expectancy or less than 10% value remaining after asset development, or is subsequently used in other SR&ED).

body.text: Critical Rules for Restored Capital Property:

items: Exclusions: Under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and 37(8)(e), land, leasehold interests in land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, inventory, and goodwill are strictly excluded.

New vs. Used Equipment Distinction: Both new and used ASA depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, may be included 100% in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures on Line 390 (and must not be claimed for regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 unless the claimant fails to claim it on Form T661 by the 18-month reporting deadline). However, for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9), the property must be new when acquired (never used, acquired for use or lease, or demonstrated for a prior purpose by a previous owner). If used equipment is refurbished by a vendor to such a significant extent that its useful life is restored comparable to new equipment, the purchase qualifies for ITCs; if the claimant refurbishes its own used SR&ED equipment after December 15, 2024, only the refurbishment costs qualify.

Non-Arm's-Length Purchases & Refundability: Under subsection 127(11.6), the qualified expenditure for capital property purchased from a non-arm's-length supplier is capped at the cost incurred by the NAL party. Qualifying new ASA capital property earns the 35% enhanced ITC (for CCPCs and ECPCs within the $6,000,000 limit), which is 40% refundable in cash.

body.text: 2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504 and Boxes 788–796 of Form T661)

Depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities—and therefore does not meet the 90% ASA intent test—may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under paragraphs (a)(iii) and (c) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). To qualify, the property must be new, must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations (such as buildings, property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes, or property used in the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility/plant/line), and must not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF).
Unlike ASA capital property (which is evaluated on intended use at acquisition), SUE qualification is evaluated on actual operating time:

items: First Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): The First Period begins when the property becomes available for use (subsection 13(27)) and ends at the end of the first taxation year that occurs at least 12 months after acquisition. If the equipment is actually used primarily (more than 50%, but less than 90%) of its total operating hours for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period, 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21 and deemed capital costs under subsections 13(7.1)/(7.4), and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6) and assistance under subsection 127(18)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC.

Second Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): The Second Period begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year that occurs at least 24 months after acquisition. If the property qualified as First Term SUE and was used primarily (more than 50%) of its actual operating hours for SR&ED in Canada across the Second Period, a further 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC—for a cumulative maximum of 50% of capital cost across the two periods.

Pool, CCA, and Form T661 Reporting: SUE capital cost is never included in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the full cost under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8 (and any SUE ITC claimed reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost [UCC] of the CCA class in the subsequent year). On the May 15, 2026 version of Form T661, SUE is claimed on Line 504 and detailed for the 20 most expensive items in Box 788 (name of property), Box 790 (purchase date), Box 792 (25% of capital cost), Box 794 (first-term "1" or second-term "2"), and Box 796 (project numbers).

body.text: 3. Restored Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

The CRA's official SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026) and SR&ED Updates confirm that lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, are once again allowable under both the Traditional and Proxy methods (for any taxation year straddling December 16, 2024, the SR&ED usage percentage is calculated based on total operating time after December 15, 2024):

items: Under the Proxy Method: If leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost may be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)). If leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used more than 50% but less than 90% (primarily) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost may be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)). If leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% can be claimed under the Proxy Method. Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, lease costs for GPOEF and the lease of land cannot be claimed (as they are covered by the 55% PPA).

Under the Traditional Method: If leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease expenditure is claimed as a lease cost (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)). If leased equipment is used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the proportional percentage of the lease expenditure used for SR&ED may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures (along with land leases), provided it is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(c).

Building vs. Structure Leases: Under paragraph 37(8)(d)(ii) and subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i), lease costs for the use of, or right to use, a building are excluded under both methods—except for lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada under section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations. Where a single lease covers both a building and equipment, the claimant must make a reasonable allocation between the non-allowable building and the allowable equipment; lease costs for non-building structures (such as a bridge or dam) may also qualify.

body.text: 4.6 Unpaid Amounts (The 180-Day Rule) and ITC Recapture (20-Year Window)
Unpaid Amounts (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))
Accrued SR&ED expenses are policed by two strict 180-day payment rules:

items: Unpaid Salaries and Wages (Subsection 78(4)): Employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days from the end of that taxation year is excluded from SR&ED salaries for that year, and is instead deemed to be an expenditure incurred in the subsequent year when paid (identified on Line 310 of Form T661, where it is excluded from the PPA salary base).

Unpaid Other Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26)): Current expenditures (other than salary/wages, such as contracts or materials) incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days after the taxation year-end are deemed not to have been incurred in that year and must be deducted when calculating total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes. Crucially, unpaid amounts must be identified on Form T661 on or before the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the year incurred; any unpaid amount not identified by that 18-month deadline will never be included in qualified SR&ED expenditures, even when paid in a subsequent year. For an unpaid arm's-length contract expenditure, in the year incurred the claimant first reduces the contract by 20% and then deducts the remaining 80% as an unpaid amount (yielding $0 qualified expenditure in that year); in the subsequent year when paid, 80% of the paid amount is added to qualified expenditures.

body.text: Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act, ITC Recapture reverses all or a portion of an SR&ED ITC by adding the recaptured amount directly to the claimant's Part I tax payable when four conditions are met:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36) for ITCs earned in 1998 and subsequent taxation years);

The cost of the property was a qualified expenditure (such as materials transformed into a prototype/custom asset, restored ASA capital property, or SUE—noting that salaries, wages, and overhead are never subject to recapture);
A percentage of the cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of a taxation year; and

In the year, the claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use (when the asset becomes available for use in earning income under subsection 13(27)) the property or another property incorporating it.

body.text: Key Recapture Rules and Exceptions:

items: Calculation of Recapture: The recapture is the lesser of the ITC originally obtained for the property and the applicable ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or Fair Market Value [FMV] upon conversion to commercial use or NAL disposition; for SUE where both First and Second Term credits were claimed, the ITC rate is applied to 50% of the proceeds of disposition or FMV, or 25% if only First Term SUE was claimed).

Shared-Use Equipment Conversion Threshold: For SUE, a conversion to commercial use does not occur unless SR&ED usage becomes only incidental—that is, when the property has been all or substantially all (ASA, 90%+) converted to commercial use.

De Minimis 10% Scrap Rule: Under CRA administrative policy, no recapture is applied where proceeds from the scrap sale of an experimental product (or the FMV at conversion/NAL disposition, or insurance proceeds for materials consumed) are less than 10% of the total cost of the property.

Non-Arm's-Length Dispositions and Transfers: Disposing of SR&ED capital property to a NAL purchaser (or transferring property under a subsection 127(13) NAL contract) does not immediately trigger recapture if the property continues to be used ASA (90%+) for SR&ED by the transferee; recapture occurs under subsections 127(29), 127(33), 127(34), or 127(35) only when the property is later sold or converted to commercial use. Any ITC recaptured in a prior year is added back to the claimant's subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the following year.

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

In Canada, nine provinces and one territory (Yukon) offer statutory R&D tax credits that layer on top of the federal SR&ED program. Only three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec via the CO-17 corporate return) and Alberta (administered by the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration via the AT1 corporate return), all other provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are co-administered by the CRA through schedules filed with the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive: Quebec's Modernized CRIC Regime (Sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31)

In the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget Plan and Quebec Finance Information Bulletin 2025-6, the Government of Quebec enacted a major structural reform of its innovation tax system. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished eight separate innovation tax measures—including the former Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) under section 1029.7 (Form RD-1029.7, which had provided a 14% base to 30% enhanced credit on wages up to $3,000,000), the tax credit for university or public research centre research, the tax credit for pre-competitive private partnership research, and the tax credit for research consortia membership fees—and consolidated them into the single Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), governed by sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Quebec Taxation Act.
As detailed in Quebec government and tax practitioner analyses of the enacted CRIC regime, its core mechanics operate as follows:

items: Refundable 30% Enhanced and 20% Base Rates: The CRIC is 100% refundable. It provides an enhanced rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and a base rate of 20% on all eligible expenditures beyond that $1,000,000 limit. The $1,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit must be shared among associated corporations using Form RD-1029.8.EN and prorated based on the number of days in the year for a short taxation year. Where the credit is claimed by a corporation as a member of a partnership, the 30% enhanced rate does not apply.

Exclusion Threshold (Minimum $50,000): Before any credit is earned, eligible expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of (i) $50,000 (prorated for short taxation years) or (ii) an amount calculated using the Quebec basic personal amount applicable to the employees involved in the eligible activities.

Eligible Activities (R&D and Pre-Commercialization) and Expenditures: Unlike legacy R&D credits that stopped at the end of experimental development, the CRIC covers both scientific research and experimental development (R&D) carried out in Quebec and pre-commercialization activities carried out in Quebec as a continuation of R&D (such as testing, prototyping, and technological validation). Eligible expenditures include salaries paid to employees directly engaged in eligible activities (including directly related support roles), 50% of arm's-length subcontractor contracts reasonably attributable to work performed in Quebec (requiring disclosure of the subcontractor's identity and Quebec Sales Tax [QST] number or Social Insurance Number), certain payments to eligible research organizations, and new depreciable capital property used in Quebec almost exclusively for eligible activities (excluding land, buildings, or rights in a building).

Filing Requirements and Federal Interaction: Claimants must file Form RD-1029.8.CR with their CO-17 Quebec corporate income tax return (or within 12 months after the CO-17 filing deadline), reporting the credit on the CO-17 return using code 112 for the R&D portion and code 113 for the pre-commercialization portion, alongside Form RD-222 to claim the tax deduction for R&D expenditures. Any CRIC received or receivable in respect of SR&ED constitutes provincial government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure base under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal ITA.

body.text: 5.3 Deep-Dive: Ontario's Dual-Grind Mechanics and Federal Assistance Stacking

In Ontario, corporate claimants must navigate three sequential calculations across the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), and the federal SR&ED ITC:

items: Step 1 — Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566 / T2SCH31): The OITC is an 8% refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum annual credit of $240,000). The $3,000,000 expenditure limit phases out if the corporation's (and associated group's) preceding-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or if preceding-year taxable paid-up capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. As illustrated in specialist Ontario tax credit guidance, where both phase-out ranges are triggered, the surviving percentages multiply rather than taking the lesser of the two: for instance, at $700,000 of prior-year taxable income (leaving $1,000,000 or 1/3 of the $3,000,000 limit) and $30,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (leaving $20,000,000 ÷ $25,000,000 = 80% of the limit), the surviving OITC expenditure limit is $1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000, yielding a maximum 8% OITC of $64,000.

Step 2 — Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508 / T2SCH31): The ORDTC is a 3.5% non-refundable credit with no expenditure cap (unused balances carry back 3 years and forward 20 years against Ontario corporate income tax). Crucially, under Ontario law, the OITC is treated as government assistance that reduces the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC. Therefore, on $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no other grants:
OITC = 8% × $1,000,000 = $80,000 (refundable);
ORDTC = 3.5% × $920,000 = $32,200 (non-refundable);
Combined Ontario Credits = $80,000 + $32,200 = $112,200 (an effective combined Ontario credit rate of 11.22% of the eligible pool).

Step 3 — Federal Subsection 127(18) Assistance Grind: Under subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, both the refundable OITC ($80,000) and the non-refundable ORDTC ($32,200)—including the portion of those provincial credits earned on the notional 55% PPA—are provincial government assistance that reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (unless renounced on time). Subtracting $112,200 from $1,000,000 leaves a federal ITC base of $887,800. At the 35% enhanced federal ITC rate, this yields $310,730 in federal ITCs, for a total combined federal and Ontario benefit of $422,930 (42.293% of the $1,000,000 qualified pool).

body.text: 6. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, and the 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process
6.1 Dual-Stream Administrative Governance and RTA Review Standards

The federal SR&ED program is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), while legislative policy and special-purpose building approvals reside with the Department of Finance Canada. Within the CRA, technical eligibility is evaluated by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) supervised by Research and Technology Managers (RTMs), while expenditure costing is audited by Financial Reviewers (FRs) under the Financial Claim Review Manual.
Under the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, RTAs are bound by strict administrative and evidentiary standards:

items: Impartiality and Non-Negotiation: RTAs must make decisions that are fair, impartial, and respectful of current legislation and CRA policy, and must never negotiate eligibility or expenditures.

Procedural Fairness and Transparency: RTAs must explain the review process, identified issues, and documentation requirements in plain language, allow claimants to present their position and submit additional information, and consider all submitted information before reaching a final decision.

Weighing the Evidence: RTAs apply the principle of weighing the evidence, recognizing contemporaneous evidence—documents created at the time the work was performed as a direct result of doing that work—as the most reliable form of proof.

Mandatory RTM Consultations: An RTA is required to consult with their Research and Technology Manager (RTM) before recommending disallowance due to lack of information, making an unfavourable decision without an on-site visit, considering penalties or suspected fraud, issuing formal "better books and records" letters, or making significant changes to an approved review plan.

body.text: 6.2 The New Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Effective April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Effective April 1, 2026 (announced in a CRA news release on April 8, 2026, following its introduction in the Canada Strong Budget 2025), the CRA launched its new optional Pre-Claim Approval process, succeeding the earlier 2016 Pre-Claim Consultation and Pre-Claim Review pilot programs. Pre-claim approval allows eligible businesses to have their planned (or recently begun) R&D work evaluated by the CRA before incurring significant costs or filing their tax return.

To qualify for pre-claim approval, the business must (i) be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or Canadian partnership, (ii) have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and (iii) be in good standing with the CRA. Furthermore, the application can cover a maximum of 3 projects, and each project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation.
The pre-claim approval workflow proceeds through four structured steps:

items: Step 1 — Request a Case Number: The business submits a five-minute online web form on Canada.ca. Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing are contacted within 2 business days through My Business Account with a case number; all other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by telephone.

Step 2 — Complete and Upload Form T1322: The applicant completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval)—providing business identification (Lines 010–016), project title, anticipated start date, and estimated total SR&ED expenditures (Lines 020–024), strict word-limited technical descriptions of the uncertainty, initial hypothesis, and planned experiments/analyses in Section B, and preparer and signing officer certifications (Lines 050–082)—and uploads the application via My Business Account.

Step 3 — Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist (RTA) Within 4 Weeks: Within 4 weeks of submitting the application, the CRA assigns an RTA to review the file. For new SR&ED claimants (and any business not in good standing), a 2-to-5-hour meeting with the RTA (virtual via videoconference/mobile camera facility tour, or in person) is mandatory; for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, the RTA may request a meeting at their discretion.

Step 4 — Written Determination Within 8 Weeks and 90-Day Expedited Review: Within 8 weeks of submitting the completed application in My Business Account, the RTA issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report providing the rationale for the decision. If approved, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years (unless material changes are made to the project). Crucially, when the claimant later files its SR&ED tax claim containing pre-approved projects and that claim requires an expenditure review, the CRA's processing time is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days.

body.text: 6.3 Prescribed Forms (Form T661 Parts 1–10), the 20 Largest Projects Rule, and Part 9 Penalties

To access SR&ED tax incentives, a claimant must submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, specifically providing prescribed information in Parts 2, 3, 8 to 17, 24, and 25) for corporations or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for individuals and trusts. Claimants using tax preparation software to file electronically must not also mail paper copies of Form T661 (and if a federal agency has designated a project as "classified information" for national security reasons, Section B of Part 2 is kept on a separate sheet on-site rather than submitted with the return, following the special CRA national security letter procedure).
Form T661 is organized into 10 parts:

items: Part 1: General corporate or claimant information;

Part 2 (Sections A to C): Project-by-project technical descriptions (with strict word limits in Section B) and Line 207 requiring the Canada Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 field of research (FOR) code for each project. Under the 20 Largest Projects Rule, claimants may choose to submit Part 2 with their filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided the cost of every project is included in Part 6 and completed Part 2 descriptions for all projects are maintained at the claimant's place of business and provided to the CRA upon request (failure to provide them upon request results in disallowance of those projects' expenditures);

Part 3 (Sections A to C): Calculation of allowable SR&ED expenditures (Line 360 overhead, Line 380 current expenditures, Line 390 restored capital expenditures, Line 400 total allowable expenditures) and the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures;
Part 4: Calculation of qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (including Line 504 and Boxes 788–796 for Shared-Use Equipment, and Line 535/540 adjustments);
Part 5 (Sections A and B): Calculation of the salary base and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA);
Part 6: Project costs allocated on a project-by-project basis for all claimed projects;
Part 7: Additional information;
Part 8: Claim checklist;

Part 9: Claim Preparer Information—mandatory disclosure for each claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim, including billing arrangements. While Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline and missing or inaccurate information in Part 9 will not disallow the SR&ED claim itself, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed if the prescribed information about the claim preparer(s) and billing arrangement(s) is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable; and
Part 10: Certification signed by the authorized signing officer of the corporation or individual.
