6.4 The Strict 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (Subsections 37(11), 127(9)(m), and 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the year in which the expenditure was incurred, with no statutory mechanism for extension under subsection 220(2.2):

items: Corporations (18 Months After Tax Year-End): A corporation's T2 return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year; adding 12 months yields a strict reporting deadline of 18 months after the taxation year-end. If a corporation's tax year ends on the last day of a month (e.g., February 28), the T2 return is due on the last day of the 6th month (August 31) and the SR&ED reporting deadline is the last day of the 18th month (August 31 of the following year); if the tax year ends on a specific calendar day (e.g., January 6), the T2 return is due on the same day of the 6th month (July 6) and the SR&ED reporting deadline is the same day of the 18th month (July 6 of the following year).
Trusts (90 Days + 12 Months): A trust's T3 return is due no later than 90 days after the trust's tax year-end, making its SR&ED reporting deadline 12 months after that 90-day due date.

body.text: Consequences of Late Filing: A letter expressing an "intent to file" an SR&ED claim does not satisfy the statutory filing requirements. If Form T661 or the required prescribed information is submitted after the 18-month reporting deadline, the claimed expenditures are denied as SR&ED expenditures: the claimant cannot deduct them or include them in its subsection 37(1) pool and cannot earn any ITCs. If Form T661 is filed on time by the 18-month deadline, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the 18-month deadline, the claimant is still permitted to include the allowable SR&ED expenditures in its subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but is disqualified from earning any ITC on those expenditures.
7. Landmark Judicial Precedents and Tax Court Case Law Analysis

Disputes over CRA technical or financial reassessments are initiated by filing a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Division within 90 days of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment (or appealing directly to the Tax Court of Canada within 90 days of the assessment or Notice of Confirmation). In the Tax Court of Canada, taxpayers may elect the flexible Informal Procedure if the disputed federal tax/credit does not exceed $25,000 per assessment (or $50,000 per loss determination), or proceed under the General Procedure, with further appeals on questions of law lying to the Federal Court of Appeal within 30 days of the Tax Court judgment.
7.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)

items: Court and Judge: Tax Court of Canada, Judge Donald G.H. Bowman (as he then was), judgment dated May 1, 1998 (Docket 97-531(IT)G).

Facts and Issue: The appellant, an engineering consulting firm specializing in river engineering, environmental studies, hydrology, storm water management, and physical hydraulic modelling, appealed the Minister's denial of SR&ED tax credits across hydraulic modelling and river engineering projects.

Legal Holding: Judge Bowman ruled in favour of the appellant, holding that the work qualified as SR&ED and setting out at paragraph 16 the foundational five-criterion legal test for SR&ED eligibility in Canada:
Technical Risk or Uncertainty: Is there a technical risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Technological Advance: Did the process result in a technological advance, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding?
Contemporaneous Record Keeping: Although the Income Tax Act and the Regulations do not say so explicitly, a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept as the work progresses.

body.text: 7.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, (1998), 99 D.T.C. 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA)

items: Court: Federal Court of Appeal, judgment dated December 21, 1998 (Docket A-710-96).

Facts and Issue: The taxpayer conducted experimental development involving testing by its engineer (Mr. Slonimsky, who died prior to trial) and his assistant. Although the Tax Court judge made two key factual findings—first, that testing had been undertaken, and second, that the research efforts constituted a technological advancement—the Tax Court judge denied the claim on the basis that the taxpayer failed to produce written documentation proving "repeatability" of the experiments.

Legal Holding: The Federal Court of Appeal endorsed the five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic, confirmed that systematic research includes testing, and reversed the Tax Court's dismissal. At paragraph 16, the Court held that once the trial judge found that testing had been undertaken and that a technological advancement had been achieved, a rebuttable inference was raised that the testing was carried out in accordance with Regulation 2900, making it an error to impose an additional evidentiary burden of proving "repeatability" through written records.

body.text: 7.3 C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (FCA) & Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, (1997), 97 D.T.C. 724 (TCC)

items: Legal Holdings: In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393, December 2001, affirming 2000 D.T.C. 2372 (TCC)), the Federal Court of Appeal at paragraph 17 formally restated and approved Judge Bowman's five questions from Northwest Hydraulic as the standard appellate framework for SR&ED eligibility. In Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen ((1997), 97 D.T.C. 724 (TCC)), Judge Bowman established the overarching statutory interpretation principle cited across Tax Court jurisprudence (including Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21, and Clevor Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 166): because the Act's incentives for SR&ED are intended to encourage scientific research by Canadians, the legislation must be given a "fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation" in accordance with section 12 of the Interpretation Act to best ensure the attainment of that objective.

body.text: 7.4 Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2017 TCC 6

items: Court and Judge: Tax Court of Canada, Justice Sommerfeldt, judgment rendered January 2017.

Facts and Legal Holdings: In dismissing the appellant's appeal regarding theatrical rigging projects that failed to meet the scientific eligibility criteria, Justice Sommerfeldt clarified three doctrinal points frequently cited in subsequent Tax Court decisions:

Meaning of "Routine Engineering" (Paragraph 17): Acknowledged that while there is no definitive statutory definition of "routine engineering," the term typically describes "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field".
Meaning of "Hypothesis" (Paragraph 26): After reviewing the jurisprudence, concluded that a hypothesis is "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial".

Scientific Method and Contemporaneous Records (Paragraphs 33 and 46): Summarized at paragraph 33 that the scientific method requires trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. At paragraph 46, citing Justice Jorré in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313, para. 94), Justice Sommerfeldt noted that while contemporaneous documentation can be necessary to resolve factual disputes between parties, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development".

body.text: 7.5 National R & D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (Docket 2017-3837(IT)G)

items: Court and Judge: Tax Court of Canada, Justice Dominique Lafleur, judgment rendered July 7, 2020.

Facts: The appellant CCPC claimed $68,029 in SR&ED deductions and $23,810 in ITCs for its 2011 taxation year for developing a web-based "Project Tracking System" (PTS Project) to track and automate SR&ED claims using a multi-tiered architecture (ADO, Classic ASP, COM+, and Microsoft SQL Server 2000). Crucially, the company imposed self-restrictions limiting the project to legacy software tools it already owned (using SQL Server 2000 rather than SQL Server 2005, which already had a native PIVOT command) and tools with which its staff had prior experience.
Legal Holding: Justice Lafleur dismissed the appeal with costs, establishing critical rules for software SR&ED claims:

No Objective Technological Uncertainty (Paragraphs 21, 31–32): The taxpayer failed to show on a balance of probabilities that the PTS Project involved genuine technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field.

Failure to Conduct Methodical and Systematic Testing (Paragraphs 35, 48–49): Although the company's president formulated hypotheses, Criterion 2 and Criterion 3 were not met because the appellant failed to establish through a logical progression between tests that methodical and systematic testing of those hypotheses was actually conducted.

Inadequate Software Documentation (Paragraphs 51, 67–71): The appellant's "Project Timeline" and task breakdown merely tracked employee hours spent on tasks without recording hypothesis formulation, test procedures, or test results, and the submitted source code contained no revision history or multiple versions tracking test progression.

body.text: 7.6 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2021 FCA 88 & Recent Objective Uncertainty Rulings

items: Appellate Confirmation of Northwest Hydraulic (Kam-Press Metal Products, 2021 FCA 88): In Kam-Press (May 10, 2021, Docket A-442-19, affirming 2019 TCC 246), the appellant argued that because the text of subsection 248(1) contains no explicit reference to "scientific method," the Tax Court erred in applying the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Webb rejected this argument, citing RIS-Christie (99 D.T.C. 5087), C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355), and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152), and reaffirmed that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) (further applied by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2026 in Tuna Temple, 2026 FCA 175).

Objective vs. Subjective Technological Uncertainty (Dave's Diesel Inc., June 2022 TCC & JEC Distributors Inc., December 2022 TCC): In both Dave's Diesel Inc. (para. 28) and JEC Distributors Inc. (paras. 22–23), the Tax Court of Canada emphasized that the technological uncertainty criterion is an objective test, not a subjective test based on the limited training of the claimant's personnel: "The Appellant rests its case on the subjective knowledge of the four non-engineers and non-mechanics who worked on the project. To them, every aspect of the project was a 'technological uncertainty'. The 'technological uncertainty' standard, however, is not subjective. If it were subjective, a grade school student trying to build a simple electric motor would meet the test." Claimants must prove that the risks could not be overcome by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field (and as noted in Paveit Construction Inc., September 2025 TCC, para. 40, failing to lead expert or objective technical evidence makes establishing system uncertainty over routine engineering particularly challenging).

cells: SR&ED legislation must be given a "fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation" under s. 12 of the Interpretation Act to encourage Canadian research.

Software SR&ED: legacy tool constraints & unversioned source code

Challenge to the "scientific method" criterion under s. 248(1)
Unanimously confirmed that Northwest Hydraulic's 5 criteria (including the scientific method) remain binding law interpreting subsection 248(1).
Technological uncertainty is strictly an objective standard measured against competent professionals in the field, not the subjective skill level of the claimant's internal staff.

body.text: 8. Interaction with Direct Innovation Grants and Government Assistance Rules

Canadian innovators frequently combine SR&ED claims with direct government grants, contributions, and partnerships such as NRC IRAP (National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program), Mitacs, NSERC Industrial Research Chairs, CanExport Innovation, or provincial loans/grants such as Ontario's Advanced Manufacturing and Innovation Competitiveness (AMIC) stream. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, any government assistance (assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect government funding delivered through a non-profit entity—in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance, other than the federal SR&ED ITC) or non-government assistance (an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance included under paragraph 12(1)(x)) that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its filing due date reduces both the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis.
Key Audit Mechanics for Grant and Loan Stacking

items: Accrual Recognition of Assistance: Assistance is recognized on an accrual basis in the taxation year in which the claimant has received it, is entitled to receive it (because required conditions have been fulfilled), or can reasonably be expected to receive it.

Preservation of the 55% PPA Salary Base When Receiving Salary Grants (e.g., NRC IRAP): While a government salary grant such as NRC IRAP reduces the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18), the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy confirms that the salary base under Regulation 2900(4) is calculated on eligible salaries and wages before deducting government salary grants. Consequently, the claimant still earns the full 55% notional PPA on the grant-funded SR&ED salaries, and the grant reduces only the net qualified expenditure pool once.

Forgivable and Conditionally Repayable Government Loans: Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government funding arrangements with conditional repayments (for example, where repayments are contingent on future product revenues reaching a threshold, or where a loan is partially forgivable such as AMIC loans that are up to 30% forgivable to $500,000) are treated by the CRA in full as government assistance rather than ordinary business loans, thereby reducing both the subsection 37(1) pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year received or receivable.

Repayments of Government Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(c)): When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED claim, the repayment increases the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(c) and is added back to the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool to earn an ITC at the historical ITC rate from the taxation year in which the assistance originally reduced the claim. However, because repayments of assistance are not defined as "qualified expenditures," the ITC earned on a repayment is non-refundable in the year of repayment (though it may be applied against Part I tax payable, carried back 3 years, or carried forward 20 years).

body.text: 9. Comprehensive Numerical Audit Walkthrough (2026 Taxation Year)

To demonstrate the exact statutory interaction of the post-December 15, 2024 federal rules enacted under Bill C-15 alongside the Ontario OITC and ORDTC regimes, consider a Canadian-controlled private corporation (InnovateCan Corp.) with a December 31, 2026 taxation year-end, $8,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (below both the $15,000,000 federal threshold and $25,000,000 Ontario threshold), and $250,000 in prior-year taxable income (below the $500,000 Ontario threshold). During 2026, InnovateCan Corp. carries out a single eligible experimental development project exclusively at its Ontario facility, elects the Proxy Method, and pays all expenses within 180 days of year-end:

items: Incurred 2026 Expenditures:
Non-Specified Employee SR&ED Salaries (100% directly engaged): $800,000.
One Specified Employee (100% directly engaged, employed 365 days in 2026): Paid $250,000 base salary plus a $50,000 bonus ($300,000 total).
Materials Consumed in SR&ED Testing: $100,000.
Arm's-Length Canadian Subcontractor Invoice for SR&ED: $150,000.
New Specialized SR&ED Testing Machine (Acquired Feb 1, 2026, intended 95% ASA for SR&ED): $200,000.
Government Grant (NRC IRAP) Received for Non-Specified Employee Salaries: $100,000.

body.text: Step-by-Step Audit Computation

items: Step 1 — Eligible SR&ED Salaries and 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA):
Non-Specified Employees: $800,000 enters both the direct salary pool and the PPA salary base.

Specified Employee Direct Salary Pool: The $50,000 bonus is excluded. The $250,000 base salary is below the 2026 5 × YMPE cap ($74,600 × 5 = $373,000), so $250,000 enters the direct SR&ED salary pool.
Total Direct SR&ED Salaries: $800,000 + $250,000 = $1,050,000.

Specified Employee PPA Salary Base (Regulations 2900(7)): Restricted to the lesser of 75% of base salary ($250,000 × 75% = $187,500) or 2.5 × YMPE for 2026 ($74,600 × 2.5 = $186,500). Thus, the specified employee's PPA salary base is capped at $186,500.
Total PPA Salary Base: $800,000 + $186,500 = $986,500.
55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): $986,500 × 55% = $542,575.
Step 2 — Gross Qualified SR&ED Expenditures and Grant Reduction:

Direct SR&ED Salaries ($1,050,000) + 55% PPA ($542,575) + Materials Consumed ($100,000) + 80% of Arm's-Length Subcontractor ($150,000 × 80% = $120,000) + New ASA Capital Equipment ($200,000) = $2,012,575 gross qualified expenditures.
Subtracting the $100,000 government salary grant leaves $1,912,575 in net eligible expenditures before provincial credits ($1,712,575 current/PPA portion and $200,000 capital portion).
Step 3 — Ontario OITC (Schedule 566) and ORDTC (Schedule 508):
Assuming Ontario's mirroring of federal qualified expenditures applies across the $1,912,575 pool:
OITC (8% Refundable, $3,000,000 cap): $1,912,575 × 8% = $153,006 (100% refundable).
ORDTC Base (Reduced by OITC): $1,912,575 − $153,006 = $1,759,569.
ORDTC (3.5% Non-Refundable): $1,759,569 × 3.5% = $61,585 (applied against Ontario tax payable or carried forward up to 20 years).
Total Ontario Credits: $153,006 + $61,585 = $214,591.

body.text: 10. Audit Readiness and Contemporaneous Documentation Best Practices

In accordance with the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and the Tax Court of Canada's rulings in Northwest Hydraulic, Joel Theatrical Rigging, National R & D Inc., and Dave's Diesel Inc., claimants should implement five internal controls as their R&D work progresses:

items: Frame Technological Uncertainties Objectively Against the State of the Art: Avoid describing commercial objectives, product features, self-imposed legacy tool constraints, or subjective employee skill gaps in Part 2 of Form T661. Document why established design methods and standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field were insufficient—highlighting interlocking system constraints, parameters outside normal operating ranges, or non-conforming specifications.

Maintain Versioned Experimental Records Linked to Hypotheses: As National R & D Inc. Technical teams should maintain version-controlled repositories, test logs, photographs of prototypes, and analytical records that capture each hypothesis formulated, the specific experiments or analyses run to test it, quantitative results, and the logical conclusions that guided subsequent iterations.

Track Employee Hours Contemporaneously by Activity Type: Keep contemporaneous time records allocating each technical employee's hours between (i) hands-on basic research, applied research, or experimental development, (ii) directly supporting work across the eight paragraph 248(1)(d) categories, and (iii) excluded commercial production, quality control, style changes, or general administration.

Log Equipment Operating Time for Post-December 15, 2024 Capital, SUE, and Leases: To substantiate restored ASA capital property (90%+ intended use), Shared-Use Equipment (more than 50% actual operating hours across the 12-month First Period and 24-month Second Period), and leased equipment (90%+ ASA or more than 50% primarily under the Proxy Method), maintain machine usage logs recording exact SR&ED operating hours versus commercial operating hours after December 15, 2024.

Utilize the April 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322): Eligible corporations and partnerships with gross business income under $25,000,000 embarking on new R&D projects should submit Form T1322 through My Business Account to obtain a written CRA technical determination within eight weeks (valid for up to three years) and reduce any subsequent expenditure review processing window from 180 days to 90 days.
